label: Courage and Fear
framing: Courage in Scripture is not the absence of fear but the presence of something stronger than fear. It is rooted not in the size of your nerve but in the promise that God goes with you, and so its command is almost always paired with a reason, be strong and courageous, for the Lord your God is with you.
cultural: The world of the Bible knew courage chiefly as the warrior's, the strength to face the spear and not break ranks, and it honored the brave above the cautious. But Scripture quietly reframed it, locating real courage less in the soldier than in the prophet who told the king a truth he did not want to hear, and in the widow, the exile, and the unarmed who stood on God's word against the powers of their day. Courage became the willingness to obey God where it cost you the crowd's approval, or your safety, or your life.
historical: The Christian story is full of this quieter courage, from the martyrs of the early centuries who would not burn incense to Caesar, to Athanasius standing against the world in the fourth century, to the believers who hid the hunted in the darkest years of the twentieth. Dietrich Bonhoeffer returned from safety in America to a Germany he knew would kill him, judging that he had no right to share in the rebuilding if he had not shared the trial. Courage, in this telling, is faith doing the next costly thing.
application: Courage is built in small acts long before any large one is asked, the hard conversation you stop avoiding, the truth you tell when silence would be easier. Do not wait to feel brave, since courage is mostly acting rightly while still afraid. Name the thing you fear out loud, which shrinks it, and remember you are not asked to be adequate to the danger but only faithful in it. And measure your courage by where it costs you something, not by where it wins you applause.

verses.text: Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid or terrified of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you; He will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verses.where: Moses, a hundred and twenty years old and about to die, tells Israel to be strong and courageous, because the LORD goes with them and will never leave them nor forsake them. The site's note says he then charges Joshua publicly with the same words. The command to be brave comes with its reason attached, and the reason is God's presence, not their strength.

verses.text: Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”
verses.where: After Moses' death God charges Joshua three times to be strong and courageous, and promises to be with him as he was with Moses. The site's note says the same charge tells him to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth and meditate on it day and night. Joshua's courage was to be fed by God's word as well as by God's promise.

verses.text: But David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.
verses.where: For forty days Goliath taunts Israel and, as the site's note says, Saul and his soldiers are paralyzed by fear. David, a young man bringing food to his brothers, goes out against him and says he comes in the name of the LORD of Hosts. His courage did not come from armor, which he refused, but from knowing whose battle it was.

verses.text: Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: “Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!”
verses.where: When Haman's decree threatens her people, Mordecai warns Esther that silence will not save her. The site's note tells how she calls for a three-day fast and resolves to go to the king unsummoned, against the law, saying if I perish, I perish. Her courage was not reckless: it began with fasting and the support of her people, and it risked her own safety for others.

verses.text: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego replied to the king, “O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king. But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”
verses.where: Commanded to bow to a golden statue on pain of the furnace, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego tell the king their God is able to deliver them, but even if he does not, they will not bow. The site's note on the chapter tells how a fourth figure was seen walking with them in the fire. Courage in Scripture does not depend on knowing how it will turn out.

verses.text: But Peter and John replied, “Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
verses.where: Ordered not to speak in Jesus' name, Peter and John answer that they cannot stop speaking about what they have seen and heard. The site's plain note says they refused one command, to stop speaking about Jesus, answered respectfully, did not resist arrest, and prayed for courage, not for revenge. It adds that the verse is not permission to disobey any law one dislikes.

verses.text: Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath), Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.
verses.where: After the crucifixion, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, goes boldly to Pilate to ask for Jesus' body. The site's note says a member of the body that condemned Jesus now takes the risk of honoring him, and the plain note says Joseph waited a long time before he was brave. Courage that comes late is still courage.

verses.text: “Come,” said Jesus. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus. But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. “You of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?”
verses.where: Peter gets out of the boat at Jesus' word and walks on the water, then sees the wind, is afraid and begins to sink, and cries out. The site's note says the rescue comes before the rebuke, and the plain note says little faith is not no faith: Peter had enough to step out and enough to cry to the right person. Brave people still sink, and the hand still reaches them.

verses.text: Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. Do everything in love.
verses.where: Near the close of his letter Paul tells the Corinthians to be alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous and strong, and do everything in love. The site's plain note says Paul joins courage and love, and asks the reader which they lean toward and which they lack. Courage without love turns hard; love without courage turns timid.

verses.text: But now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. And be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work! For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts.
verses.where: In 520 BC the builders of the second temple think their work looks like nothing beside the old one, and God tells the governor, the high priest and all the people to be strong and work, for he is with them. The site's note says the message comforts builders who were discouraged. Some courage is not for a battle but for keeping on with ordinary work that seems small.

misread.taken: I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength is printed on shirts and quoted before games and interviews as a promise that faith will bring success at whatever a person sets their mind to.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul wrote it from prison, not from a stage, and that the all things are the things he has just named: being filled and being hungry, having plenty and having need. The strength Christ gives him is the strength to be content. The verse is not a slogan for ambition or a promise of success; it is a prisoner's peace, which a person who has lost a job, a game, their health or their plans can still say truly.
misread.text: I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.

whole: Courage is needed in more ordinary places than battlefields. To say the hard thing in a meeting. To report what a colleague is doing. To tell a family secret to a counselor. To walk into a hospital room, a courtroom, a church after years away. To apologize first. To stand up for someone being mocked, or to say no to a group that expects a yes. Most people who lack courage are not cowards in general. They are afraid of particular things: being disliked, being alone, being wrong, losing a job or a place. And many assume that brave people simply do not feel what they feel.

Scripture's brave people were afraid. Joshua was told again and again to be strong and courageous, because there was much to fear. Saul's whole army was paralyzed while one young man went out. Esther explained to Mordecai exactly why going to the king could kill her. Peter walked on the water and then sank. Joseph of Arimathea, the plain note says, waited a long time before he was brave. What made them brave was not a fearless temperament but where they looked: to the God who goes with them, to whose battle it was, to what they had seen and heard. Our own cowardice usually has a reason we can name, and most of us have kept quiet when speaking would have cost us something we wanted to keep.

So the Bible's wisdom is to find courage in God's presence rather than in our nerve, and to use it for love. The command to be strong almost always comes with a reason: the LORD your God is with you. Prepare as Esther did, with prayer and the support of others, and then act. Speak the truth plainly and respectfully, as the apostles did before the council, without contempt for those who oppose you and without treating every rule you dislike as a test of faith. Keep courage joined to love, as Paul does, so that it does not turn hard. And remember that courage is often quiet: staying near someone in trouble, finishing ordinary work that seems small, taking the next step while still afraid.

The hope Scripture gives is that the courage God asks for, he also gives. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did not know whether they would be delivered, and they were not alone in the fire. Peter sank, and Jesus' hand reached him before the word did. Jesus himself was afraid in Gethsemane and went to the cross, and he has overcome the world. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is trust that keeps walking, because the one who goes with you will never leave you nor forsake you.
deep.sit: Where is God asking you to be brave right now, and what is the one fear that keeps you from it?

prayer.lead: The end of a psalm that moves from confidence to anguished prayer and back. The site's plain note says it ends before the answer comes, and says wait patiently for the LORD twice, because once is rarely enough.
prayer.text: Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living. Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!
